'''''Euphorbia prostrata''''' is a species of [[Euphorbia|spurge]] known by the common name '''prostrate spurge''' or '''prostrate sandmat'''.

It is native to the [[Caribbean]], most of [[South America]], [[Central America]], [[Mexico]], and most of the [[United States]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Euphorbia prostrata Aiton {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:101913-2 |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Euphorbia prostrata (prostrate sandmat): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/euphorbia/prostrata/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref>. It is widely [[introduced species|naturalized]] in many other parts of the world, where it can be found in varied habitat types, and in many areas grows as a roadside weed<ref name=":1" />.

==Description==
''Euphorbia prostrata'' is an annual herb producing slender prostrate stems up to approximately {{convert|20|cm}} long, sometimes purple-tinted in color.<ref>[http://www.aluka.org/action/showMetadata?doi=10.5555/AL.AP.FLORA.FZ7275&pgs=&cookieSet=1 Aluka Profile]{{dead link|date=July 2015}}</ref> The oval-shaped leaves are up to {{convert|1|cm|spell=in}} long with finely toothed edges.

The [[inflorescence]] is a [[cyathium]] less than {{convert|2|mm|spell=in}} wide, with white petal-like appendages surrounding the actual flowers. There are four male flowers and a single female flower, the latter developing into a lobed, hairy fruit {{convert|1|to|2|mm|spell=in}} wide.

''E. prostrata'' is similar to both ''[[Euphorbia maculata]]'' and ''[[Euphorbia serpens]]'', but is often hairy on the leaves and stems, while the latter two species are often smooth. It differs from ''E. maculata'' by its less elongated and less lanceolate leaves. ''E. serpens'' by contrast has much more rounded leaves than ''E. prostrata'' with relatively larger and more conspicuous flowers. The flowers of ''E. prostrata'' do not typically show the white "petals" seen in ''E. serpens'' or ''E. maculata'' and thus flowers are hard to detect in the former species. Only ''E. maculata'' shows dark spots in the center of each leaf, but this is not always present in that species.

==Medicinal use==
''Euphorbia prostrata'' extract has been found effective for treatment of bleeding [[hemorrhoids]] due to its contents of flavonoids, phenolics and phenolic acids.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bakhshi|first1=Girish D.|last2=Langade|first2=Deepak G.|last3=Desai|first3=Vidyadhar S.|title=Prospective, Open Label Study of Euphorbia Prostrata Extract 100 mg in the Treatment of Bleeding Haemorrhoids|journal=Bombay Hospital Journal|date=2008|volume=50|issue=4|pages=577–583|url=http://www.bhj.org/journal/2008_5004_october/download/page-577-583.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306014857/http://www.bhj.org/journal/2008_5004_october/download/page-577-583.pdf|archive-date=March 6, 2012|access-date=July 31, 2015}}</ref> ''Euphorbia prostrata'' extract tablets have been marketed in India and the US by [[Panacea Biotec]] Ltd.
